evidence: Receiving DO2 collapses from 10.27 mg/L (46.0 h) to 1.69 mg/L (46.2 h) and remains 1.0-1.7 mg/L through 52 h, below the 2.0 mg/L minimum
Source batches source-1/2/3 show minimum DO2 of ~7.4-8.0 mg/L over equivalent 96 h runs; receiving vessel behaves differently and cannot rely on source precedent
Receiving P assay: 0.99 g/L at 36 h, 2.57 g/L at 48 h (available 52 h), showing the process is in its productive phase during the DO deficit
Source P at 48 h: 2.98-3.06 g/L — receiving is on-track prior to the DO2 excursion, arguing against stop or strong feed cuts that would forfeit product mass
args.rationale: At 46.2 h the receiving fermenter's DO2 crashed from ~10.3 to ~1.7 mg/L and has stayed at ~1.0-1.7 mg/L through the 52 h decision time, well below the 2.0 mg/L minimum oxygen constraint. This indicates oxygen demand exceeded transfer capacity (unlike source batches, which never fell below ~7.4 mg/L). A bounded combined intervention — feed ×0.8 to reduce oxygen uptake and aeration ×1.15 to increase supply — restores the DO balance from both sides while keeping the culture productive. Keeping DO2 above the minimum protects further product accumulation (P rose 0.99 g/L @36 h to 2.57 g/L @48 h and must continue to retain counted production). Stop would yield zero counted production; strong_feed_reduction (×0.6) would over-restrict a process that was performing normally before the excursion; feed reduction or air increase alone leaves insufficient margin given the magnitude (~9 mg/L) of the DO drop.
args.uncertainty: The hidden cause and magnitude of the OUR spike at ~46 h are unknown; if demand is much larger than estimated, ×1.15 air/×0.8 feed may only partially restore DO, requiring escalation later. Conversely, if the excursion was a transient sensor/equipment artifact, the mild combined action carries only small productivity cost. Source data cannot fully calibrate receiving OTR; no physics tool output was relied upon.
